tts_text: to conquer. to occupy. to annex. an annex. to colonize.

senses.definition: Defeat a people or army and gain control of their land by force.
senses.example: The army conquered the neighboring kingdom.

synonyms.note: for overcoming an opponent; defeat alone does not always imply taking territory
for fears and difficulties

antonyms.note: for yielding to an opponent rather than overcoming it

senses.definition: Successfully overcome a fear, difficulty, or other obstacle.
senses.example: She conquered her fear of public speaking.

situations.situation: An army gains and then holds control of a city.
situations.examples: The army conquered the city. / The army occupied the city.
situations.guidance: Both may describe the same conflict. Conquer emphasizes defeating resistance and gaining control; occupy emphasizes holding the place.

situations.situation: A country claims a neighboring region as part of itself.
situations.examples: It occupied the region but did not annex it.
situations.guidance: Military control does not automatically mean incorporation into the country. Annex describes that claim or incorporation, without implying international recognition.

situations.situation: An outside power establishes a colony.
situations.examples: The power conquered the territory and later colonized it.
situations.guidance: Conquer highlights military victory; colonize highlights establishing a colony through settlement or outside rule. These actions can overlap and need not occur in this order.

situations.situation: You describe ordinary work or personal challenges.
situations.examples: The migration occupied most of our time. / She conquered her fear of speaking in meetings.
situations.guidance: Occupy also concerns space, roles, time, and attention. Conquer also means overcome a difficulty; annex and colonize do not normally replace them here.

comparison.note: All four can concern territorial control, and several may describe the same event. Conquer emphasizes gaining control through defeat; occupy emphasizes control or presence; annex emphasizes adding or claiming territory as part of a political unit; colonize emphasizes establishing a colony. They are not a fixed sequence. Annex also names a building addition or document supplement; colonize also describes organisms establishing themselves in a habitat.

senses.common_patterns: conquer + city/territory/kingdom; conquer a fear; conquer a difficult challenge.

senses.definition: Fill or use a space, or hold a position.
senses.example: The cabinet occupies most of the room.

synonyms.note: for space; not a substitute in every role context
for time
for a person; requires a different construction
also has broader nonmilitary uses

senses.definition: Keep someone busy or use their time or attention.
senses.example: The migration occupied most of our time that week.

senses.definition: Take or maintain control of a place, especially with armed forces.
senses.example: Foreign troops occupied the city.

senses.common_patterns: occupy + place/space/position; occupy most of the room; occupy a senior role. She occupies a senior position at the company. Occupy someone’s time/attention; occupy yourself with + noun/V-ing. Keep yourself occupied = keep yourself busy.

senses.definition: Add or claim territory as part of a country, state, or city, often by taking control of it.
senses.example: The empire annexed the border region.

synonyms.note: broader; normally incorporate the territory into a larger political unit
for a building addition; an annex may also be a separate nearby building
for supplementary document material; institutional naming practices vary

antonyms.note: for giving up territory to another power

senses.common_patterns: annex + territory/region; annex an area to a country. Noun: an annex to a building/report; in the annex. American spelling: annex for both noun and verb.

senses.definition: An additional building or part of a building used with a main building.
senses.example: The library keeps its archives in a separate annex.

senses.definition: A supplementary section attached to a document, especially an official report or agreement.
senses.example: The technical requirements are listed in an annex to the agreement.

senses.definition: Establish a colony in a place, through settlement or control by an outside population or power.
senses.example: Several European powers colonized territories overseas.

synonyms.note: overlaps in settlement contexts but does not itself imply colonial rule
requires a plural subject and a different construction

senses.definition: For organisms, establish a population in a new place or habitat.
senses.example: Bacteria quickly colonized the exposed surface.

senses.common_patterns: colonize + territory/island/planet; bacteria/plants colonize a surface/habitat. Related nouns: colony; colonization.

informal noun; written with a hyphen

situations.situation: You tell a friend you were sick.

situations.situation: Your stomach contracts but nothing comes up.

situations.guidance: Retch names the straining action. Dry heaving is retching without bringing anything up; retching can also precede vomiting.

situations.situation: A bird brings food back up to feed its chicks.
situations.examples: The bird regurgitated food for its chicks.
situations.guidance: Regurgitate emphasizes bringing swallowed food back up. This can be normal feeding behavior and does not necessarily mean illness.

situations.situation: An answer repeats material without showing understanding.
situations.examples: He regurgitated the documentation instead of explaining the design.
situations.guidance: This figurative sense of regurgitate is critical. Vomit, retch, and throw up do not have this ordinary information-repetition sense.

comparison.note: Vomit and throw up overlap closely for bringing stomach contents out through the mouth; their main everyday difference is register. Retch emphasizes the movements or effort, often without expelling anything. Regurgitate emphasizes food returning to the mouth and also has a useful disapproving sense for repeating information without understanding or processing it. Retch is mainly a recognition target here.

senses.common_patterns: vomit; vomit blood; feel like vomiting. Vomit is also an uncountable noun for what comes up.

senses.definition: Material brought out of the stomach through the mouth.
senses.example: There was vomit on the floor.

senses.definition: Make the straining movements of vomiting, often without bringing anything up.

synonyms.note: specifically when nothing is expelled

senses.common_patterns: retch; start/keep retching; make someone retch. Usually used without a direct object.

senses.definition: Bring swallowed food back up into the mouth.
senses.example: The bird regurgitated food for its chicks.

synonyms.note: a descriptive phrase; regurgitation need not involve illness

senses.definition: Repeat information or ideas without properly understanding or processing them; disapproving.

senses.definition: Vomit; conversational.

synonyms.note: more neutral; common in medical contexts

senses.common_patterns: throw up; throw up your food; throw it up. Use threw up for the past tense and thrown up after have/has.

senses.definition: Move upward or increase in amount, level, or rank.

more conversational
for amounts and levels

antonyms.note: for getting up from a seat

senses.definition: Get up from sitting or lying down; often more formal than get up.
senses.example: She rose from her chair to greet the visitors.

situations.situation: You describe an increase in prices.
situations.examples: Prices rose. / The company raised its prices.
situations.guidance: Both describe an increase. Rise has no direct object; raise names the affected thing as its object and identifies a cause.

situations.situation: An issue comes up during a meeting.
situations.examples: An issue arose during the review. / I raised the issue during the review.
situations.guidance: Arise describes the issue emerging; raise describes someone bringing it up for discussion.

situations.situation: Unusual activity causes people to become suspicious.
situations.examples: The discrepancy raised suspicion. / The discrepancy aroused suspicion.
situations.guidance: Both work. Arouse emphasizes causing the reaction; do not force a distinction when both are natural.

situations.situation: You identify the source of a problem.
situations.examples: The error arose from an incorrect assumption. / The error rate rose after the deployment.
situations.guidance: Arise from introduces a source or cause. Rise describes an increase in the error rate.

comparison.note: Rise means go up or increase; arise usually means happen, emerge, or result from something. These uses have no direct object. Raise means lift, increase, or bring something up and takes an object; it also has money-raising and child-rearing senses. Arouse causes a feeling or reaction and can also mean sexually excite someone. Forms: rise–rose–risen; arise–arose–arisen; raise–raised–raised; arouse–aroused–aroused. Rise and raise also have useful noun senses.

senses.common_patterns: rise to + level; rise by + amount; rise from a chair. The sun rises. No direct object in these uses. Forms: rise–rose–risen.

senses.definition: An increase or upward movement.
senses.example: We saw a sharp rise in support requests.

senses.common_patterns: a problem/question/opportunity arises; arise from + source/cause. The error arose from an incorrect assumption. No direct object. Forms: arise–arose–arisen.

senses.definition: An increase in pay; American English.

situations.guidance: Thought-provoking describes the discussion’s effect on people; well-thought-out evaluates the preparation and reasoning behind the argument.

comparison.note: Both can positively describe ideas or material. Well-thought-out concerns careful development; thought-provoking concerns intellectual effect. A proposal can be both, and neither quality guarantees the other.

senses.common_patterns: a well-thought-out plan/proposal/strategy/argument; The plan is well thought out. Use hyphens before a noun; usually omit them after be.

senses.definition: Making you think carefully or deeply about something.
senses.example: The documentary raised some thought-provoking questions about privacy.

senses.common_patterns: a thought-provoking question/discussion/article/film; find something thought-provoking: I found her presentation thought-provoking.
